text: how did the dinosaurs die out?
spoken: Mostly an asteroid. About sixty-six million years ago, a huge rock hit what's now Mexico. It threw dust and debris into the air, blocking sunlight for a long time. Plants struggled, then the animals that ate them, then their predators. Volcanic eruptions in India were happening around then too, and scientists still discuss how much each cause mattered.

text: how did napoleon die?
spoken: Napoleon died in May 1821, in exile on the island of Saint Helena. The official cause was stomach cancer, and his autopsy showed a stomach ulcer that had gone bad. Some people have argued he was poisoned with arsenic. I'm not sure that holds up, and historians still disagree about it.

text: what killed the people at pompeii?
spoken: Mostly the eruption of Vesuvius in the year seventy-nine. Not lava, which people often assume. First came falling pumice and ash, which collapsed roofs. Then fast, scorching clouds of gas and ash, called pyroclastic surges, swept through. Those killed most people quickly, by extreme heat and by choking on ash.

text: why did socrates drink hemlock?
spoken: Because Athens sentenced him to death. In 399 BC he was convicted of impiety and corrupting the young, and hemlock was the usual method of execution. He could've proposed exile instead, but he refused, and he stayed put when friends offered an escape. Does that part surprise you?

text: why does romeo kill himself in the play?
spoken: Short version, he thinks Juliet is dead. He finds her in the tomb, looks perfectly lifeless, and can't imagine living without her. She's actually asleep from Friar Laurence's potion. The Friar's message explaining the plan never reaches Romeo, so he's working with false information. So it's a tragedy of timing and miscommunication, not just love.

text: how do antibiotics kill bacteria?
spoken: Antibiotics attack things bacteria have that your cells don't. Penicillin, for example, blocks bacteria from building their cell walls. The wall weakens, and the cell bursts. Other antibiotics jam the bacteria's protein-making machinery. Your cells' version is built differently, so you're mostly spared. Do you know why that difference matters?

text: why do leaves die in autumn?
spoken: Short days and cold tell the tree winter's coming. Leaves are costly to keep, and useless when the light is weak. So the tree seals off the leaf at its base. Chlorophyll, the green stuff, breaks down. Then yellows and oranges show through. Want to know where the reds come from?

text: how high can a cat fall and survive?
spoken: Surprisingly high, actually. Vets have documented cats surviving falls from over twenty stories, though serious injuries are common. I'm not sure of an exact limit, and it varies cat to cat. Want to see why they sometimes do better from higher up?

text: what happens to a star when it dies?
spoken: It depends on how heavy the star is. A star like our sun swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers. What's left is a small hot core called a white dwarf. A much heavier star ends in a supernova explosion. The core left behind becomes a neutron star, or for the heaviest ones, a black hole.

text: how long can a whale hold its breath?
spoken: It depends on the whale. Most big baleen whales manage ten to twenty minutes. Sperm whales go longer, around an hour or more on deep dives. The record I know of is Cuvier's beaked whale, over two hours. They hunt deep squid, so they've evolved for it.

text: can you die from holding your breath?
spoken: Short answer, no, not on purpose. Your body forces you to breathe first. When carbon dioxide builds up, your brain triggers a strong urge to breathe. If you push past it, you can pass out. Then your breathing restarts on its own. The real danger is in water, where passing out can mean drowning.

text: how fast does a bullet train go?
